title: The Meter Is a Light
hook: Red on the ramp. A white line.
scene: Overcast morning at the foot of an I-5 on-ramp. A two-head signal hangs over a painted white stop line — a freeway ramp meter, not an intersection. The light is red. A sedan is already past it, running the acceleration stretch. Yuna clicks once and does not explain the rest. The kit in the back does not care if you roll a red here. The white line does.
decision: The ramp meter is red. What do you do?

options.text: Roll through — it is not a real light, just a suggestion for busy hours
options.result: You treat a red like weather. The sedan ahead never expected a second car on the same green. Ramp meters work like regular signals. You spent that.

options.text: Stop at the white stop line. When it turns green, continue up the on-ramp
options.result: You hold the line. Red stays red. Green comes. She clicks once. You use the rest of the ramp the way it was built — search, match, merge. The white line did the teaching.

options.text: Stop under the signal, then creep around it on the shoulder to skip the wait
options.result: The shoulder is a post and a drain. You left the white line to steal a green that was not yours.

options.text: Wait until two greens so you and the next car go up together
options.result: One green is one car. You held a second cycle and made a pair on a ramp built for singles. The meter was already the rule.

debrief: Red means stop on the white line. Green means continue up the on-ramp. Green gave the ramp back.

source.psdp_skill: Skill eleven: highway driving – part one
source.teaching_target: LOCKED. Cite 4.11's Freeway ramp meters child, not the parent. Red = white stop line; green = continue up the on-ramp.
source.stat_cited: DOL p.113: Ramp meters work like regular traffic signals. When the light is red, stop at the white stop line. When the signal turns green, you can continue along the on-ramp.
